questions.title: Why does GRPO apply token‑level importance ratios when the reward is defined for the whole sequence?
questions.question_body: In Section 2 the paper defines the GRPO objective (Eq. \eqref{equ:grpo}) using token‑wise importance weights $w_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}$, yet the advantage $\widehat{A}_{i}$ is computed from a sequence‑level reward $r(x,y_i)$. I would have expected an importance weight that matches the unit of the reward (i.e., a sequence‑level weight). Is there a theoretical reason why GRPO still uses token‑level weights, or is this simply an oversight that leads to the instability described later?

questions.title: How does the sequence‑level importance ratio $s_i(\theta)=\bigl(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_i|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_i|x)}\bigr)^{1/|y_i|}$ satisfy the principle of importance sampling?
questions.question_body: The paper states that $s_i(\theta)$ "aligns with the basic principle of importance sampling" (Section 4). In standard importance sampling we have $\mathbb{E}_{z \sim \pi_{	ext{beh}}}\bigl[ \frac{\pi_{	ext{tar}}(z)}{\pi_{	ext{beh}}(z)} f(z) \bigr] = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \pi_{	ext{tar}}}[f(z)]$. Here $z$ corresponds to a full response $y$, so I would expect the weight $\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y|x)}$ without any exponent. Why do we raise it to $1/|y|$, and does this preserve unbiasedness?

questions.title: What is the purpose of length‑normalization ($^{1/|y_i|}$) in $s_i(\theta)$ and how does it reduce variance?
questions.question_body: Equation (5) defines $s_i(\theta)$ with an exponent $1/|y_i|$. The authors claim this prevents dramatic fluctuations when only a few tokens change likelihood and puts all responses into a "unified numerical range". Could someone explain analytically how this normalization controls variance compared to using the raw sequence likelihood ratio?

questions.title: Why are the clipping ranges for GSPO ($3\times10^{-4}$–$4\times10^{-4}$) three orders of magnitude smaller than those for GRPO (0.2–0.27)?
questions.question_body: Both algorithms use a clip function $\mathrm{clip}(r,1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$, yet Table 1 reports vastly different $\varepsilon$ values for GSPO versus GRPO. Is this difference solely due to the magnitude of $s_i(\theta)$ versus $w_{i,t}(\theta)$, or are there other factors influencing the appropriate clipping range?

questions.title: How does the gradient estimator derived for GSPO relate to REINFORCE with a baseline?
questions.question_body: The gradient expression in Eq. (9) looks like an expectation over sampled responses of $s_i(\theta) \widehat A_i \nabla_θ \log \pi_θ(y_i|x)$. In classic REINFORCE we have $ (r - b) \nabla_θ \log \pi_θ(y)$. Is $s_i(θ)$ acting as an additional weighting factor beyond a baseline? Does this affect bias or variance compared to standard REINFORCE?

questions.title: Why does GSPO‑token use `sg` (stop‑gradient) on $s_i(θ)$ when defining $s_{i,t}(θ)$?
questions.question_body: In Eq. (13) the authors define $s_{i,t}(θ)= \mathrm{sg}[s_i(θ)] \cdot \frac{π_θ(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}{\mathrm{sg}[π_θ(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})]}$, where `sg` denotes detach (no gradient). Since numerically this equals $s_i(θ)$, what is the purpose of stopping gradients on both terms? How does this affect back‑propagation compared to simply using $s_i(θ)$ directly?

questions.title: How does GSPO avoid the need for Routing Replay in Mixture‑of‑Experts models?
questions.question_body: Section 6·2 explains that in GRPO, expert activation volatility makes token‑level ratios unstable, prompting the authors to cache routing decisions (Routing Replay). GSPO instead computes only sequence‑level ratios $s_i(θ)$ and claims this eliminates sensitivity to routing changes. Could someone clarify why aggregating over tokens makes the method insensitive to per‑token routing volatility?

questions.title:
What happens if all rewards in a group have identical values, making $\,	ext{std}\bigl(\,
group r(x,y_i)\bigr)=0$?
questions.question_body:
The advantage estimator $
̂A_i = \frac{r(x,y_i)-\,	ext{mean}(\,
group r)}{ \,	ext{std}(\,
group r)}$ would be undefined when the standard deviation is zero (e.g., all sampled responses receive reward 0). How do the authors handle this edge case in practice?

questions.title: Does partitioning a large rollout batch into multiple mini‑batches introduce off‑policy bias for GSPO, and how is it mitigated?
questions.question_body: In Section 6·1 each rollout batch is split into four mini‑batches for gradient updates. Since samples are drawn from an older policy but are used multiple times before updating $π_θ$, could this cause additional off‑policy discrepancy beyond what clipping already handles? Are there any theoretical or empirical measures taken to keep such bias low?

questions.title: Why does clipping a much larger fraction of tokens not harm training efficiency in GSMO compared to GRPO?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 shows that GSPO clips roughly two orders of magnitude more tokens than GRPO yet achieves higher training efficiency (faster reward improvement per compute). Intuitively I would expect discarding more data reduces sample efficiency. What explains this counter‑intuitive result—does sequence‑level clipping provide a better signal despite fewer effective tokens?

questions.title: Can we combine GSPO’s sequence‑level clipping with PPO’s KL regularization term, and what would be the effect?
questions.question_body: The PPO objective in Eq.~(1) includes a KL regularizer which was omitted for brevity; many RLHF pipelines keep it to prevent policy drift. Does adding a KL penalty on top of Eq.~(7)’s clipped sequence objective preserve stability gains while further controlling divergence from a reference model? Has anyone studied this combination?

questions.title: How should GSPO be adapted for multi‑turn RL where rewards may be assigned after each turn rather than only at episode end?
questions.question_body: GSPO-token is introduced as a way to adjust advantages per token, but multi‑turn conversations often have turn‑level feedback (e.g., after each system response). Would it make sense to compute separate advantages per turn while still using a sequence‑level importance ratio? How would one correctly formulate such an objective without breaking the theoretical justification provided for Eq.~(7)?
